headline: Where'd the Blues Go? Chasing the Bunker Schools from Ocean City to Townsends
subhead: The blitz we flagged last week finally rolled into South Jersey water — but the real lesson this week is in the tide charts, not the boils.
body_markdown:
How many of you called me this week asking the same question: "Darnell, is it worth driving to the beach before work, or should I wait for the evening tide?" Fair question, and it's the right one to be asking right now, because the answer changes by the hour with this bait migration we're in the middle of.

Let's start with the receipts. We told you last week that the bluefish blitz working down from North Jersey would keep pushing south as the bunker schools tracked the beach, and that's exactly what happened. By Wednesday there were peanut bunker balls getting pinned against the Ocean City boardwalk beaches and down through Sea Isle City on the incoming tide, with blues from cocktail size up to six and seven pounds crashing through them in the wash. Same story off Townsends Inlet — the bait comes down the beachfront on the push, gets squeezed against the jetty rocks, and the blues pile in for twenty, thirty minutes at a stretch before it goes quiet and moves on. If you're fishing it, don't waste time on big topwater plugs when the water's boiling — a simple 1-ounce Kastmaster or a Gotcha plug fished on wire leader will get bit as fast as anything, and you don't lose your whole tackle box to bluefish teeth.

Here's the classroom part. Surf and inlet water is sitting in the mid-to-upper 70s right now, and that's well outside where striped bass want to be — their comfort zone runs 68 to 72 degrees. So while the blues are thriving in this warm water, the bass have gone the other direction: deep, structure-oriented, and mostly nocturnal. If you want a striper this week, your best window is full dark to first light, working bunker chunks or eels on the bottom at Absecon Inlet along the rock pile on the outgoing, or drifting the deeper rip off Great Egg Inlet where the current digs a trench close to 25 feet. I had a report of a mid-20-inch fish and one better one pushing 30 inches coming off cut bunker fished tight to bottom on the last two hours of the ebb at Absecon — that's your program until the water cools.

Fluke are the dependable lesson plan this time of year, and they haven't disappointed. The sod banks off Brigantine are still holding fish in that 8 to 15 foot depth range, and the pattern hasn't changed all summer — drift with the outgoing tide as it pulls bait out of the marsh creeks, dragging a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail tipped with a strip of squid. You're going to catch plenty of shorts doing this, but the keepers are mixed in, especially on the last two hours of the ebb when everything funnels out of the back bay channels. Absecon Inlet's channel edges, 20 to 30 feet on the drop-offs, have been holding better average size — fish to 5 pounds reported this week on the same bucktail-and-Gulp combo, though you'll need enough lead to hold bottom against that inlet current, so bump up to an ounce or an ounce and a quarter on a strong tide.

Weakfish have been a quiet bright spot for the guys fishing at night. If you're working the back bay channels under the lights at the Route 52 causeway or the bridges through Ocean City, small soft plastics like a 4-inch Storm Shad on a light jig head have been picking up weakfish in the 16 to 20 inch class mixed in with the white perch and small stripers. It's not a numbers game, but it's a nice change of pace after a day of bluefish teeth and short fluke.

Surf regulars working the troughs at Ocean City and down toward Stone Harbor have kept kingfish coming steady on bloodworms and Fishbites fished on a high-low rig, best around the morning high tide when the wash is calm enough to hold bottom without a ton of lead. And for the guys who like to fish the jetty rocks at Absecon Inlet, this is prime time for triggerfish — small ones mostly, but they'll hammer a piece of clam or sand flea fished tight to the rocks in that 4 to 8 foot zone, and they're a fun distraction between bluefish runs.

Looking ahead, the tide is still running strong off that recent full moon, but it'll start easing toward neap by midweek, which usually means the bait disperses a little and those tight, explosive blitz windows spread out and get harder to predict. I'd expect the bluefish pattern to hold through the weekend if the southwest wind stays put and the water stays warm, but don't be surprised if the boils get shorter and more scattered by Tuesday or Wednesday. If a cold front does slide through later in the week like some are expecting, watch for it to shuffle the deck — a quick drop in surface temp could push bait tight to structure again and give the striped bass a reason to feed a little earlier than 11 p.m. That's the kind of shift worth adjusting your whole evening around, so keep an eye on the sky before you plan your tide.
